title: Onion Gravy
subtitle: Rich, deeply flavoured onion and stock gravy
excerpt: Sweet, deeply caramelised onions cooked down in stock and a splash of wine until the gravy is thick, glossy, and savoury. The essential partner for sausages, roast meats, and toad in the hole.

recipe.sourceNotes: Onion gravy is a staple accompaniment in British cooking, served with roast meats, sausages, toad in the hole, and all manner of potato dishes. Unlike a pan gravy (made from roasting juices), onion gravy is a free-standing sauce built from deeply caramelised onions and stock. The depth of colour and flavour depends entirely on taking the onions far enough in the caramelising step: they should be a deep mahogany brown, much darker than they look as they begin to soften. This takes at least 20 minutes of patient cooking, stirring frequently, and represents the flavour foundation of the whole dish. Cutting the onions with the grain (from root to tip) rather than across them produces long strips that caramelise more evenly. The thickening is provided by a small amount of flour, which must be cooked briefly to eliminate any raw taste before the stock is added.

recipeTools.notes: A wide saucepan or saute pan.

content.text: Take the onions further than feels right. They should be a dark, sticky, mahogany brown: if they are a pale gold, the gravy will lack depth and colour. Add a splash of water or wine if the onions look like they are catching and burning rather than caramelising. The total caramelising time is at least 20 minutes, and usually closer to 25 to 30 for a truly deep flavour.

items.preparation: halved and thinly sliced with the grain
or vegetable stock for a vegan version

content.text: Heat the oil in a wide saucepan over medium-high heat. Add the onions and a pinch of salt. Cook for 5 minutes, stirring, then reduce to medium-low heat. Cook for 20 to 25 minutes, stirring regularly, until the onions are very dark and sticky.

Increase the heat to medium. Add the flour and stir for 1 minute. Add the wine and let it bubble for 1 minute. Pour in the stock, add the thyme, bay, and Worcestershire sauce. Bring to a simmer and cook for 10 minutes until thickened.
Season and remove the herb sprigs. The gravy should be thick, glossy, and coating. Serve immediately or keep warm over very low heat.
